The welfare loss from a merger is proportional to the premerger price elasticity of demand and the premerger market share of the merging parties, and the merger will be anticompetitive if the premerger demand elasticity is sufficiently low.
the anticompetitive effect of a merger is increasing in the degree of concavities in both demand and costs.

(i) The anticompetitive effect of mergers is greater the more concave the demand; (ii) the anticompetitive effects of mergers are greater the more elastic demand is in the short-run, but less elastic in the long-run; and (iii) the anticompetition effects of mergers depend on the number of firms in the market, and the more firms there are in the market the less anticompetitive the effects of mergers.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the elasticity of demand is a useful tool for assessing the anticompetitive effect of mergers, provided that the elasticity of substitution between products is greater than one and the elasticity of demand for the merged product is smaller than the elasticity of demand in the premerger industry.
, in the absence of information on the degree of competition in the market, the premerger demand elasticity should be used to determine whether the merger will be welfare improving or not.
, when demand is concave, the premerger market share of the merging firms is a sufficient condition to assess the welfare effect of a merger, as it implies that the post-merger price will increase.
